newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Revised data raises Argentina's 1991-94 GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Revised data raises Argentina's 1991-94 GDP growth.

text.p: An official revision of Argentine statistics shows the economy grew at an average 8.9 percent a year in the boom years of 1991-1994, rather than the 7.7 percent previously estimated, analysts said Friday.

"We were growing at Asian rates and we didn't even realize it," said one economist -- while calculating that by the same yardstick the Tequila recession meant gross domestic product shrank by 4.6 percent last year, rather than 4.4 percent.
An official document released this week said an update of data carried out by the Central Bank "has led to modifications in the series."
The alterations are due to newly available data, changes in estimation proceedures and the incorporation of calculations on economic activities that were not previously included.

The revised data indicates that from 1991, when President Carlos Menem's Peronist government launched its Convertibility plan pegging the peso to the dollar, until 1994, the economy grew 40.4 percent versus the 34.8 percent previously estimated, said analysts at the Broda and Proeco consultancies.

"The new estimates do not change the composition of the factors but the levels, which are higher -- which raises the estimate of gross domestic product," said Macreconomica consultancy's analyst Nicolas Dujovne.

Macroeconomica estimates that the most important changes of data are in consumption, investment and exports. In the 1990-94 period these three categories grew at 10 percent, 25 percent and 3.6 percent respectively, rather than the 8.7 percent, 22 percent and 2.2 percent previously estimated.
Analysts believe that this new data raises 1995's GDP, at current values, by about 6.0 billion pesos from the 285.5 billion pesos previously estimated.
For the 1990-95 period, the revised data gives a GDP growth rate of 6.0 percent versus the previous 5.2 percent.
